name: Dubrow Diet

card.summary: An interval-eating (time-restricted) plan by Terry and Heather Dubrow, marketed for weight loss and a leaner, younger-looking appearance.
card.note: Dietitians advise people with a history of disordered eating to avoid it.

quick.overview:
The Dubrow Diet is a plan from plastic surgeon Terry Dubrow and his wife, Heather Dubrow, published as a 2018 book. It uses fixed daily eating windows, a form of intermittent fasting they call interval eating, to help people lose body fat and look and feel younger.

The appeal for looks is leanness and facial and body slimming. No clinical trial has tested the Dubrow Diet itself; dietitians quoted in the press note that intermittent-fasting research is mostly short-term or small.
quick.how: The plan has three phases: a short jump-start with an 8-hour eating window and 16-hour fast, a weight-loss phase with windows from 8 to 12 hours, and a maintenance phase with a 12-hour window most days and stricter 8-hour days. It also specifies food choices.
quick.risks: Dietitians quoted by NBC News said calories in the first phases are below what most experts recommend and advised against it for people with eating-disorder histories. As with any calorie-restricting plan, those with medical conditions are generally told to consult a clinician.

lead: The Dubrow Diet is an interval-eating plan described in the book The Dubrow Diet: Interval Eating to Lose Weight and Feel Ageless (2018, Ghost Mountain Books) by Terry Dubrow, a plastic surgeon known from television, and Heather Dubrow.[1] A follow-up, The Dubrow Keto Fusion Diet, appeared in 2020.[1]
It is aimed at weight loss and an ageless look, and Wikipedia describes it as a fad diet based on intermittent fasting.[1] It limits eating to a daily window of 8 to 12 hours.[2]
No published clinical trial has tested the plan. Dietitians commenting in the press describe intermittent-fasting research as mostly short-term, small or in rodents.[2]

chain: Daily eating window and set food choices
Lower body fat, slimmer face and body
angle.text: The plan aims at leanness, which changes facial and body contours; its authors also market it as supporting an ageless appearance.

paras: Phase 1, 'Red-Carpet Ready', is a two-to-five-day jump-start with an 8-hour eating window and 16-hour fast. Phase 2 lets users choose a window from 8 hours (with a cheat day) to 12 hours depending on goals. Phase 3 is maintenance with a 12-hour window five days a week and two stricter 8-hour days.[2]

Registered dietitian Samantha Cassetty told NBC News that she liked the emphasis on produce but found calorie levels in the first two phases lower than most experts recommend and portions restrictive, and she called the focus on appearance and 'before body' language outdated.[2] She noted that intermittent-fasting studies tend to be short-term, small or in rodents, and advised against the plan for anyone with an eating-disorder history.[2]

timeline.event: The Dubrow Keto Fusion Diet published.[1]
